questions.question: Define a design brief, contrast a brief that states a problem with one that states a solution using an example, and name the three things from the investigation that the brief must carry.
questions.expected_answer: A design brief is a short statement of the problem to be solved, naming the problem, the people affected, the setting and the purpose of the solution while leaving the form of the solution open, so any competent designer could take it up. 'Design a cardboard takeaway box' states a solution and closes off alternatives; 'food stalls at the taxi rank serve meals in polystyrene containers that block the stormwater drains and never break down; design a way of serving take-away meals at the rank that leaves no persistent waste and that owners and customers will accept' states the problem and allows a material change, a returnable container, a collection system or a change in serving to be compared. The brief must carry the worst harm shown by the evidence, the real users, and the real setting with its limits.

questions.question: Describe the two routes to a solution with an example of each, explain how the forces topic supports the first route, and state how the stage at which the harm occurs guides the choice.
questions.expected_answer: Adapting the material keeps the product but changes what it is made of or how the material is treated or combined, for example bagasse or recycled paperboard replacing polystyrene, or a single recyclable plastic replacing a laminated wrapper; the forces topic supports it because the new material must still resist the compression of stacking, the bending of a lid, the shear of a fork and softening when hot and wet, so candidates are tested for those forces. Designing a product changes the thing or adds one to the system, for example a deposit-backed returnable container, a drain guard, a reusable carrier or a rack selling meals in the customer's own container. If the harm sits in raw materials or disposal of an otherwise sound product, adapt the material; if it sits in use or the surrounding system, design a product; many strong solutions combine both, and the brief should not fix on one before sketching.

questions.question: Distinguish specifications from constraints with two examples of each, state the tests a good specification must pass, and show how a specification can be linked to a force.
questions.expected_answer: Specifications say what the solution must do and be, such as holding a 500 gram meal with gravy for 30 minutes without leaking, and stacking twenty high; constraints are limits it must stay within, such as costing no more than fifty cents more per meal and needing no electricity, water or bins at the rank. A good specification is measurable so it can be tested yes or no, traceable to a need found in the investigation or from the users, and important enough that failing it would leave the user or environment worse off. Linking to a force: 'stacks twenty high' puts the walls and base in compression, so they must not buckle; 'full lid does not sag' is bending, favouring corrugated board on edge; 'resists a fork' is puncture and shear.
